questions.chapter: Discrete-Time Signals and Systems
questions.text: State and prove the Nyquist Sampling Theorem for bandlimited continuous-time signals. For an analog signal $x_a(t) = 3\cos(100\pi t) + 2\sin(250\pi t)$, determine the Nyquist sampling rate and the reconstructed continuous-time signal when sampled at $f_s = 200 \text{ Hz}$.
questions.solutionOutline: Nyquist rate f_N = 2 f_max. Frequencies: f1 = 50 Hz, f2 = 125 Hz => f_max = 125 Hz. Minimum Nyquist rate = 250 Hz. When sampled at f_s = 200 Hz, f1 = 50 Hz is below folding frequency (100 Hz). The 125 Hz component aliases to |125 - 200| = 75 Hz. Reconstructed signal becomes x_r(t) = 3 cos(100 pi t) + 2 sin(150 pi t - pi/2).

questions.chapter: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and FFT Algorithms
questions.text: Define Circular Convolution of two finite-duration sequences $x_1(n)$ and $x_2(n)$ of length $N$. Explain how linear convolution can be computed using circular convolution and describe the Overlap-Add and Overlap-Save block convolution methods for filtering long audio sequences.
questions.solutionOutline: Circular convolution y(n) = sum x1(m) x2((n-m) mod N) corresponds to point-by-point product of DFTs: Y(k) = X1(k) X2(k). Linear convolution of lengths L and M requires zero-padding to N >= L + M - 1. Overlap-Add decomposes input into non-overlapping blocks, circular convolves each with h(n), and overlaps/adds tail ends. Overlap-Save uses overlapping input segments and discards corrupted initial points.

questions.chapter: Z-Transform and Analysis of LTI Systems
questions.text: State and prove the Initial Value Theorem and Final Value Theorem for unilateral Z-transforms. Determine the inverse Z-transform of $X(z) = \frac{1}{(1 - 0.5z^{-1})(1 - 2z^{-1})}$ for: (a) stable system, (b) causal system, and (c) anti-causal system, clearly showing regions of convergence (ROC).
questions.solutionOutline: Initial value x(0) = lim_{z -> infty} X(z). Final value lim_{n -> infty} x(n) = lim_{z -> 1} (1 - z^(-1)) X(z). Poles at z = 0.5 and z = 2. Partial fractions: X(z) = (-1/3)/(1 - 0.5z^(-1)) + (4/3)/(1 - 2z^(-1)). (a) Stable requires unit circle in ROC (0.5 < |z| < 2): x(n) = -(1/3)(0.5)^n u(n) - (4/3)(2)^n u(-n-1). (b) Causal: |z| > 2. (c) Anti-causal: |z| < 0.5.

questions.chapter: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and FFT Algorithms
questions.text: Derive the Radix-2 Decimation-in-Frequency (DIF) Fast Fourier Transform algorithm. Draw the complete 8-point butterfly signal flow graph, explain bit-reversal indexing, and compare computational complexity with direct DFT ($O(N^2)$ vs $O(N \log_2 N)$).
questions.solutionOutline: DIF splits output frequency points into even and odd indices: X(2k) and X(2k+1). First stage computes N/2 point additions/subtractions followed by twiddle factor multiplications W_N^n. Input is in natural order; output is in bit-reversed order. Reduces complex multiplications from N^2 = 64 to (N/2) log2 N = 12 for N = 8.

questions.chapter: Design of Digital Filters (FIR and IIR)
questions.text: Explain the design of digital Chebyshev Type-I lowpass filters. Derive the Chebyshev polynomial $C_N(\Omega) = \cos(N \arccos \Omega)$ and formulate how filter order $N$ and cut-off frequency $\Omega_c$ are obtained from given passband ripple ($\alpha_p$) and stopband attenuation ($\alpha_s$) specifications.
questions.solutionOutline: |H(j Omega)|^2 = 1 / [1 + epsilon^2 C_N^2(Omega / Omega_p)]. Equiripple in passband, monotonic in stopband. Parameter epsilon = sqrt(10^(0.1 alpha_p) - 1). Order N = arccosh(sqrt((10^(0.1 alpha_s) - 1) / epsilon^2)) / arccosh(Omega_s / Omega_p). Bilinear transformation maps analog Chebyshev poles to digital z-plane poles.

questions.chapter: Design of Digital Filters (FIR and IIR)
questions.text: Explain the Frequency Sampling Method for designing FIR digital filters. Derive the relationship expressing filter impulse response $h(n)$ in terms of frequency response samples $H(k)$. How is transition band optimization applied to minimize stopband ripple?
questions.solutionOutline: Samples frequency response H(e^(j omega)) at N equidistant points omega_k = 2 pi k / N: H(k) = H(e^(j 2 pi k / N)). Impulse response h(n) = (1/N) sum_{k=0}^{N-1} H(k) e^(j 2 pi k n / N). Abrupt discontinuity at cutoff causes high Gibbs ripples; transition band optimization inserts unconstrained sample values T1, T2 in transition band to maximize stopband attenuation.

questions.chapter: Design of Digital Filters (FIR and IIR)
questions.text: Compare Window Functions used in FIR filter design: Rectangular, Hanning, Hamming, and Blackman windows. Contrast main lobe width, peak side lobe attenuation (dB), and transition bandwidth trade-offs.
questions.solutionOutline: Rectangular: main lobe 4 pi / M, side lobe -13 dB (poor stopband attenuation). Hanning: main lobe 8 pi / M, side lobe -31 dB. Hamming: main lobe 8 pi / M, side lobe -41 dB (excellent general-purpose balance). Blackman: main lobe 12 pi / M, side lobe -58 dB (steepest stopband rejection, widest transition width).

questions.chapter: Design of Digital Filters (FIR and IIR)
questions.text: Compare Impulse Invariance Method and Bilinear Transformation Method for IIR filter design. Explain the mapping from continuous $s$-plane to discrete $z$-plane, aliasing limitations, and the frequency warping effect in Bilinear Transformation with pre-warping formula $\Omega = \frac{2}{T} \tan\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)$.
questions.solutionOutline: Impulse Invariance preserves time-domain impulse response: h(n) = T_s h_a(n T_s); maps vertical strips of s-plane to z-plane causing severe aliasing for non-bandlimited filters. Bilinear transformation uses trapezoidal integration s = (2/T)(1 - z^(-1))/(1 + z^(-1)), mapping entire j-Omega axis nonlinearly to unit circle e^(j omega). Eliminates aliasing but introduces frequency warping, compensated by pre-warping analog critical frequencies.

questions.chapter: Z-Transform and Analysis of LTI Systems
questions.text: Explain causality and BIBO stability criteria in the Z-domain. For a discrete-time system described by difference equation $y(n) - 0.9 y(n-1) = x(n) + x(n-1)$, determine system function $H(z)$, pole-zero plot, impulse response $h(n)$, and frequency response magnitude $|H(e^{j\omega})|$.
questions.solutionOutline: H(z) = (1 + z^(-1)) / (1 - 0.9 z^(-1)). Pole at z = 0.9, zero at z = -1. For causality and stability, ROC is |z| > 0.9 (contains unit circle => BIBO stable). Inverse Z-transform h(n) = (0.9)^n u(n) + (0.9)^(n-1) u(n-1). Frequency response evaluated on unit circle z = e^(j omega); behaves as lowpass filter.

questions.chapter: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and FFT Algorithms
questions.text: Differentiate between Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT) and Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). Explain how DFT samples DTFT and describe Spectral Leakage, Picket-Fence effect, and the role of Zero Padding in spectral analysis.
questions.solutionOutline: DTFT operates on infinite discrete sequences yielding continuous periodic spectrum in omega. DFT computes discrete frequency samples of finite sequences: X(k) = X_{DTFT}(2 pi k / N). Spectral leakage occurs when signal frequency is non-integer multiple of bin spacing. Picket-fence effect causes peak amplitude underestimation between bins. Zero padding increases DFT frequency grid density (interpolation) without increasing physical resolution.

questions.chapter: Implementation of Discrete-Time Systems
questions.text: Explain Finite Word Length Effects in digital filter implementations: Input Quantization Error, Coefficient Quantization Error, and Limit Cycle Oscillations (Zero-Input Dead-Band and Overflow Oscillations). How does saturation arithmetic mitigate overflow oscillations?
questions.solutionOutline: Real digital hardware uses finite bits. Input quantization models round-off noise as white noise. Coefficient quantization shifts pole/zero locations, risking instability in high-order poles near unit circle. Limit cycle oscillations occur in recursive IIR feedback loops: dead-band oscillations caused by round-off, overflow oscillations caused by two-complement wraparound. Saturation arithmetic clamps overflow to max/min limits, breaking overflow cycles.

questions.chapter: Implementation of Discrete-Time Systems
questions.text: Describe the architectural features of Digital Signal Processors (DSPs) optimized for high-throughput arithmetic. Compare Harvard Architecture with Von Neumann Architecture, and explain Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) units, circular addressing, and bit-reversed addressing.
questions.solutionOutline: DSPs feature Harvard architecture with separate program and data buses for concurrent memory access. Dedicated hardware MAC executes y += a * x in single instruction cycle. Circular addressing automates ring-buffer delay lines for FIR filtering without pointer reset overhead. Bit-reversed addressing provides zero-overhead pointer reordering for FFT algorithms.

questions.chapter: Discrete-Time Signals and Systems
questions.text: Explain Multirate Digital Signal Processing principles. Define Decimation (down-sampling by factor $M$) and Interpolation (up-sampling by factor $L$). Explain why an anti-aliasing lowpass filter is required before down-sampling and an anti-imaging filter is required after up-sampling.
questions.solutionOutline: Decimation reduces sampling rate: x_d(m) = x(m M). Requires digital anti-aliasing lowpass filter with cutoff omega_c = pi / M before decimation. Interpolation increases sampling rate by inserting L-1 zeros between samples, causing spectral replication (images). Requires anti-imaging lowpass filter with cutoff omega_c = pi / L and gain L to reconstruct intermediate values.

questions.chapter: Design of Digital Filters (FIR and IIR)
questions.text: Prove that an FIR filter with symmetric impulse response $h(n) = h(N - 1 - n)$ or anti-symmetric impulse response $h(n) = -h(N - 1 - n)$ possesses generalized linear phase. Classify Type-I, Type-II, Type-III, and Type-IV linear phase FIR filters and explain their frequency restrictions at $\omega = 0$ and $\omega = \pi$.
questions.solutionOutline: Linear phase ensures constant group delay tau_g = (N-1)/2, preventing phase distortion in audio/communication pulses. Type-I: symmetric, N odd, no frequency constraints (suitable for LP, HP, BP, BS). Type-II: symmetric, N even, zero at omega = pi (cannot be highpass). Type-III: anti-symmetric, N odd, zeros at 0 and pi (bandpass/differentiator). Type-IV: anti-symmetric, N even, zero at omega = 0 (highpass/differentiator).
